intro.html: Where do our traits come from? Some we are born with; some are built into a thing’s nature; some we pick up by habit or from the outside world. Scientists, historians and novelists all lean on these words when they ask whether something is nature or nurture.

Born with it: innate, congenital, hereditary (passed down in the family), instinctive (done without learning). Part of a thing’s nature: inherent, intrinsic; its opposite is extrinsic (from outside). Knowing without reasoning: intuitive. Fixed by long habit: ingrained, inveterate.

Notice how many begin with in- meaning in (not not): in-nate (born in), in-herent (sticking in), in-grained (worked into the grain). And gen (birth) shows up in congenital, just as in genes and generation.

words.def: present from birth; natural rather than learned
words.ex: Some people seem to have an {innate} sense of direction.
words.ctx: Her teachers wondered whether the girl’s musical gift was {innate} or learned, since she had hummed perfect tunes long before anyone taught her a note.
words.etym: From Latin innatus, “inborn”: in- (in) + nasci (to be born).

mn.text: Before he can even talk, Theo taps a perfect beat on his high chair with two spoons; nobody taught him: his sense of rhythm is {innate}.

scene.alt: A toddler taps a perfect beat with two spoons while his amazed mother claps.

words.def: existing as a natural, permanent part of something
words.ex: A little mess is {inherent} in finger painting.
words.ctx: Delay was {inherent} in sending letters by ship; no matter how hard the sailors worked, the crossing simply took weeks.
words.etym: From Latin inhaerere, “to stick in”: in- (in) + haerere (to stick).

mn.text: Every lemon, big or small, is sour; the sourness is in here, part of what a lemon is: it is {inherent}.

scene.alt: A boy makes a sour face biting a lemon beside a pile of lemons.

words.def: belonging to the basic nature of a thing; coming from within
words.ex: Zoe practices piano for the {intrinsic} joy of making music.
words.ctx: The old coin has little {intrinsic} value, since its metal is cheap, but collectors pay hundreds of dollars for it because it is so rare.

mn.cue: IN-trinsic: the joy comes from INSIDE
mn.text: Zoe paints all afternoon with no prize and no audience, just for the happiness it gives her: her reason is {intrinsic}.

scene.alt: A girl happily paints at an easel, hearts glowing from inside her.

words.def: coming from outside; not part of the thing itself
words.ctx: The coach worried that her players cared only about {extrinsic} rewards, such as trophies and praise, rather than about the game itself.

mn.cue: EX-trinsic: the reward comes from OUTSIDE
mn.text: Pip paints only because Victor is holding out a shiny medal for the winner; take the medal away and he stops. His reason is {extrinsic}.

scene.alt: A bored boy paints only because a man is holding up a shiny medal for the winner.

words.def: done naturally, without learning or thinking
words.ex: Pulling your hand back from a hot pan is {instinctive}.
words.ctx: No one teaches a spider how to spin its first web; the skill is {instinctive}, built in from the moment it hatches.
words.etym: From instinct, from Latin instinctus, “an urge, an impulse.”

mn.cue: in an INSTANT, no lessons needed
mn.text: The baby turtles hatch on the beach and, in an instant, head straight for the sea; no one shows them the way: the move is {instinctive}.

scene.alt: Baby turtles scurry across the sand straight toward the sea.

words.def: known or understood without reasoning it out; also, easy to understand
words.ex: The new phone was so {intuitive} that Grandma used it without reading the manual.
words.ctx: Maya had an {intuitive} grasp of geometry; she often knew the answer to a problem before she could explain how she got it.
words.etym: From Latin intueri, “to look at, consider”: in- (at) + tueri (to look).

mn.text: Rosa says “I’m fine!” with a smile, but Lila can tell at once that something is wrong; she just knows, without a single clue: Lila is {intuitive}.

scene.alt: A smiling girl with a little rain cloud over her head says she is fine, and her friend senses the truth and hugs her.

words.def: present from birth; also, being so by nature, as if born that way
words.ex: Uncle Felix is a {congenital} optimist who smiles even in a rainstorm.
words.ctx: Her honesty seemed almost {congenital}: her parents said that even as a toddler she had owned up to every cookie she took.
words.etym: From Latin congenitus, “born with”: con- (with) + genitus (born).

mn.cue: CON-GEN: there WITH him since BIRTH
mn.text: Felix has smiled at rainy days since he was a baby, and he still splashes in puddles, grinning: his cheerfulness is {congenital}.

scene.alt: A cheerful man in a raincoat jumps happily into a puddle in the rain.

words.def: firmly fixed by long habit; deep-seated
words.ex: Saying “please” and “thank you” was {ingrained} in us from an early age.
words.ctx: The habit of rising at dawn was so {ingrained} in the old farmer that, years after he sold the farm, he still woke at five every morning.

roots.means: the grain of wood or cloth

mn.cue: IN the GRAIN: it won’t come out
mn.text: Nana Lou scrubs and scrubs, but the old jam stain has soaked deep into the wood grain and won’t come out. Like an old habit, it is {ingrained}.

labels.text: IN the GRAIN: won’t come out

scene.alt: A grandmother scrubs hard at a stain soaked into a wooden table.

words.def: having a habit so long-standing that it is unlikely to change
words.ex: My aunt is an {inveterate} traveler who has visited forty countries.
words.ctx: An {inveterate} joker, Uncle Omar could not get through even a serious family meeting without at least one pun.
words.etym: From Latin inveteratus, “grown old, long-established,” from vetus (old).

mn.cue: in-VETER-ate: a VETERan of the habit
mn.text: Professor Edwin has collected stamps every week for sixty years, a true veteran of the hobby: he is an {inveterate} collector.

scene.alt: An old professor lovingly studies his stamp album beside a tall stack of albums.

words.def: passed down from parents to children
words.ex: In the old kingdom, the title of duke was {hereditary}, passing from parent to eldest child.
words.ctx: The family’s bright red hair is {hereditary}: Grandma had it, Mom has it, and now baby Rory has it too.
words.etym: From Latin hereditarius, from hereditas (inheritance), from heres (heir).

mn.cue: HEIR-editary: passed DOWN to the HEIR
mn.text: Nell, her son Pip and baby Rory all have the same bright red hair, handed down from parent to child: it is {hereditary}.

scene.alt: A red-haired mother, her red-haired son and red-haired baby stand together.

after.cap: Born with it, built in, or picked up over time.

after.html: Intrinsic motivation comes from within: you read because you love stories. Extrinsic motivation comes from outside rewards: you read to win a prize. And inveterate (a long-standing habit) is not invertebrate (an animal without a backbone).

after.name: vo-cloze

opts.s: Grandpa is an {inveterate} early riser; he has been up before the sun every day for sixty years.

after.cap: A habit of sixty years is inveterate.

items.q: Which word describes a person with a very long-standing habit?
items.why: Inveterate (from vetus, old) means long-established. An invertebrate is an animal without a backbone.

items.q: Dev studies hard only because his parents promised him a new bike for good grades. His motivation is…
items.why: The reward comes from outside, so the motivation is extrinsic.

items.q: True or false: an innate talent is one you are born with.
items.why: True. Innate comes from Latin for inborn: in + natus (born).

choices: the shape of your nose, like your father’s
items.why: Hereditary traits are passed from parents to children. Songs, scars and chess skill are picked up during life.
